data.title: Tattoo & tattoo reactions — viva
data.summary: Reactive & drug eruptions · 9 viva questions with answers
data.body:
_Viva questions for the case: **Tattoo & tattoo reactions** (Reactive & drug eruptions)_

**Q1. Classify tattoos.**
- Decorative/professional (cosmetic — permanent make-up of eyebrows, lips, eyeliner), amateur (Indian 'godna' — traditional), traumatic (asphalt/road-rash, gunpowder, coal miners, pencil lead), medical (radiotherapy marks, nipple-areola reconstruction, micro-pigmentation of scalp/vitiligo camouflage)
- Temporary: henna (natural, brownish-red) and 'black henna' (PPD-added — strong sensitiser)

**Q2. Pigments and colours.**
- Black — carbon (Indian ink), iron oxide, logwood
- Red — mercuric sulphide (cinnabar), cadmium selenide, ferric oxide, organic azo dyes (now most common)
- Yellow — cadmium sulphide; green — chromium oxide; blue — cobalt aluminate; white — titanium dioxide, zinc oxide; brown — ferric oxide; purple — manganese

**Q3. Classify tattoo reactions.**
- Acute: inflammatory (normal healing), infections — bacterial (S. aureus, Pseudomonas, non-tuberculous mycobacteria like M. chelonae from contaminated ink), viral (hepatitis B/C, HIV, HPV warts, molluscum), fungal; leprosy and syphilis historically
- Hypersensitivity: allergic contact dermatitis (red pigment commonest — cinnabar/azo), photo-allergic (yellow — cadmium), lichenoid, granulomatous (sarcoidal — may be first sign of systemic sarcoidosis), pseudolymphomatous
- Koebner phenomenon: psoriasis, lichen planus, vitiligo, DLE in tattoo
- Neoplastic: keratoacanthoma, SCC, BCC, melanoma (coincidental)
- Others: MRI-related burning/swelling (iron oxide), pigment migration to lymph nodes (mimics metastasis), 'blow-out' (pigment spread into fat), keloid

**Q4. Why is 'black henna' dangerous?**
- Contains paraphenylenediamine (PPD) to darken and speed colour — causes severe allergic contact dermatitis (blisters, hypopigmentation/keloid in the tattoo shape) and lifelong sensitisation to hair dyes, textile dyes, sunscreens (PABA), local anaesthetics (benzocaine), sulphonamides (cross-reacting para-amino compounds)

**Q5. Histopathology of tattoo reactions.**
- Pigment granules in macrophages and extracellularly in dermis; patterns: lichenoid interface, spongiotic, granulomatous (sarcoidal/foreign-body), pseudolymphomatous, pseudoepitheliomatous hyperplasia

**Q6. How do you evaluate a tattoo reaction?**
- History — colour involved, timing, sun exposure, systemic symptoms
- Biopsy; culture for mycobacteria if papulopustules within weeks; patch test (pigment series, PPD); chest X-ray/ACE for sarcoid; HBV/HCV/HIV serology for amateur tattoos

**Q7. Treatment of tattoo reactions.**
- Topical/intralesional steroids, tacrolimus; hydroxychloroquine/allopurinol for granulomatous; systemic therapy for sarcoidosis
- Excision or laser removal for persistent allergy (caution — Q-switched laser can release allergen and trigger systemic reaction)
- Antimicrobials as per culture (NTM — clarithromycin)

**Q8. Methods of tattoo removal.**
- Q-switched lasers (nanosecond) and picosecond lasers — selective photothermolysis/ photoacoustic shattering of pigment, cleared by macrophages; wavelength by colour: black — 1064 nm Nd:YAG/755 nm alexandrite; red — 532 nm KTP; green — 755/694 nm ruby
- Multiple sessions 6–8 weeks apart; the R20 method (repeated passes) and perfluorodecalin patches
- Side effects: hypo/hyperpigmentation, paradoxical darkening of cosmetic tattoos (white/flesh — titanium/iron oxide turns black), scarring, allergic reactions
- Older: excision, dermabrasion, salabrasion, CO2 laser — scar

**Q9. What is paradoxical darkening?**
- Laser reduction of ferric oxide (rust, flesh, white tones) to black ferrous oxide — common with cosmetic lip/eyebrow tattoos; test spot first

## Quick spotter facts
- Reaction confined to red part of tattoo — allergy to mercury/azo red pigment
- Black henna — PPD sensitisation
- Granulomas in tattoo — look for sarcoidosis

_Sources: Previous-year PG question papers (Sahana P Raju, Solved Papers Dermatology); IADVL Textbook of Dermatology 5e (Tattoos, foreign-body reactions). Answers written in our own words; check with your teachers' preferences._
